blocks.value: A Line Chart is one of the simplest ways to view a stock's price movement. It connects a series of price points with a continuous line. In many commonly used stock charts, the line represents the closing price for each selected period.

Imagine This: Every evening, you write down the day's temperature. At the end of the month, you mark each reading on a graph and connect the points. The line makes it easy to see whether the temperature generally rose or fell. A stock line chart works in a similar way.

Each point on the line represents the chosen price for a particular time. On a daily line chart, the point commonly represents that day's closing price. On an hourly or weekly chart, it represents the closing price of that selected period.

For example: Suppose a stock closes at ₹100 on Monday, ₹103 on Tuesday, ₹101 on Wednesday and ₹106 on Thursday. The line chart connects those four closing prices. You can quickly see the overall movement, including the small decline on Wednesday.

Line charts are useful when you want a clean view of the general direction of a stock over time. They reduce the amount of detail shown, which can make long-term movement easier to understand. This simplicity is also their limitation: a basic line chart does not show the full range of prices traded during each period.

A line chart usually does not show the opening, highest and lowest prices for each period. If you need those details, a bar chart or candlestick chart may be more useful. The right chart depends on the question you are trying to answer.
Use a line chart when you want to see the broad price direction without too much detail. Remember to check which price the line represents, usually the closing price.
